title: Manufacture of sodium hydroxide by Diaphragm Cell
topicTitle: Manufacture of sodium hydroxide by Diaphragm Cell
notes: A diaphragm cell electrolyses brine (aqueous sodium chloride) to give sodium hydroxide, chlorine, and hydrogen.
At the anode, chloride ions are discharged: 2Cl− → Cl2 + 2e−. At the steel cathode, water is reduced: 2H2O + 2e− → H2 + 2OH−.
Sodium ions move through the porous diaphragm into the cathode compartment and pair with hydroxide ions, so the cathode liquor contains NaOH.
The diaphragm keeps chlorine away from the hydroxide and from hydrogen. Chlorine mixed with sodium hydroxide forms hypochlorite and chlorate, and a chlorine-hydrogen mixture can explode.
The cathode liquor is dilute sodium hydroxide still mixed with unused sodium chloride. On evaporation, sodium chloride crystallises first and more concentrated sodium hydroxide remains.
